opening.text: Marathon runners will tell you something strange. The first mile is easy. You feel strong. The crowd is cheering. You think, I can do this all day.
Then comes mile eighteen. Your legs ache. The crowd is thinner. You start to wonder why you signed up. Some people stop there. Not because they are weak. Because the end feels too far away.

The runners who finish do not have special legs. What they have is a plan for the hard part. They keep their pace. They take water. They look at the next marker, not the finish line. And they remember why they started.
The gospel is a long race. Baptism is the starting line. It is a happy day, full of joy and promise. But the Lord does not say, "Congratulations, you are done." He says, "Now press forward."

Today I want to talk about enduring to the end. It is one of the most important parts of the gospel, and one of the least talked about. I want to share what it means, why it is hard, and how God helps us finish.

mainMessage.text: Enduring to the end means to keep going in faith, even when the road is hard. With trust in Christ and help from the Spirit, we can finish and receive eternal life.

blocks.text: What does it mean to endure to the end? The Savior used these words in a warning about the last days.
But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved.
Short and clear. Salvation goes to the one who endures. It is not enough to begin. We have to keep going.
Nephi gave a fuller picture. He had just described baptism and the gift of the Holy Ghost. Then he asked a question.

And now, my beloved brethren, after ye have gotten into this strait and narrow path, I would ask if all is done? Behold, I say unto you, Nay; for ye have not come thus far save it were by the word of Christ with unshaken faith in him, relying wholly upon the merits of him who is mighty to save. Wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life.
Is all done? Nay. That is the key. Baptism is the gate. The path is long.
Nephi gives us the recipe for the long run. Press forward. Be steadfast in Christ. Have hope. Love God and everyone. Feast on the word of Christ. And endure.
Notice that he says we got this far by the merits of Christ. We do not run alone, and we do not run on our own strength. He is the one who is mighty to save.
Why is it hard? The Lord has never pretended that the race is easy.
On the night before the cross, He told His disciples the truth.
These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.
In the world ye shall have tribulation. He does not hide it. But He pairs it with two things. Peace, that is in Him. And a fact. He has overcome the world.
Elder Richard G. Scott told us not to be surprised when trials come even to the faithful. In his talk "Trust in the Lord," from the October 1995 general conference, he said:

Testing . . . is needed even when you are living a worthy, righteous life and are obedient to \[God’s\] commandments. Just when all seems to be going right, challenges often come in multiple doses applied simultaneously.

Multiple doses, all at once. Some of us know that feeling. A health problem, a job problem, a family problem, and all in the same month. We might think, what did I do wrong? Elder Scott says testing is needed even when we are doing right.
The Lord gave Joseph Smith a promise when the trial was at its worst. Joseph was in Liberty Jail. He had cried out, asking where God was.

My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment; And then, if thou endure it well, God shall exalt thee on high; thou shalt triumph over all thy foes.

But a small moment. That is not to say it will not hurt. It says it will not last forever. And the Lord says, if thou endure it well. That is how we run the hard miles. We do not just survive. We try to endure well.
How do we endure well? The first answer is trust.
One of the best-known verses in the Old Testament says it simply.
Trust in the Lord with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.
Lean not unto thine own understanding. Many of us want to know why before we will move. Trust is when we go forward without knowing the whole map.
Elder Scott spoke about this kind of trust in the same talk. He said:

This life is an experience in profound trust—trust in Jesus Christ. . . . To trust means to obey willingly without knowing the end from the beginning (see Prov. 3:5–7). To produce fruit, your trust in the Lord must be more powerful and enduring than your confidence in your own personal feelings and experience.
Without knowing the end from the beginning. That is what we do in a marathon, too. We cannot see the finish line at mile eighteen. We trust the course.
Elder Scott also pointed to Alma and Amulek as an example. In his talk "To Be Healed," from the April 1994 general conference, he said:

The example of Alma and Amulek is enlightening. While striving to do good among the people of Ammonihah, they were taken captive. Amulek trusted his more seasoned companion, Alma, who led him to greater confidence in the Lord. Forced to observe women and children consumed by fire, Amulek said, ‘Perhaps they will burn us also.’ Alma answered: ‘Be it according to the will of the Lord’—a vital principle. ‘But . . . our work is not finished; therefore they burn us not’ \[Alma 14:12–13; emphasis added\].
Our work is not finished. That is a good line for mile eighteen. If we are still here, the Lord is not done with us.
And the Lord gives strength to those who wait on Him. Isaiah wrote:

He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength. Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall: But they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
Even the youths shall faint. It is not only the old and the tired. Everyone runs out of strength. But those who wait on the Lord get it renewed.
And Alma's people learned this in captivity. When they were in bondage, the Lord spoke to them.

And I will also ease the burdens which are put upon your shoulders, that even you cannot feel them upon your backs, even while you are in bondage; and this will I do that ye may stand as witnesses for me hereafter, and that ye may know of a surety that I, the Lord God, do visit my people in their afflictions. And now it came to pass that the burdens which were laid upon Alma and his brethren were made light; yea, the Lord did strengthen them that they could bear up their burdens with ease, and they did submit cheerfully and with patience to all the will of the Lord.
The burdens were not always removed. They were made light. The Lord strengthened them. That is how He helps us finish. Not always by taking the load away, but by helping us carry it.
Every marathon has a course. Runners who leave it get lost. How do we stay on the course in the gospel?
Lehi had a vision of a tree of life. A rod of iron ran along a path to that tree. Many in the vision wandered off. But some did not.

But, to be short in writing, behold, he saw other multitudes pressing forward; and they came and caught hold of the end of the rod of iron; and they did press their way forward, continually holding fast to the rod of iron, until they came forth and fell down and partook of the fruit of the tree.
Look at the verbs. Pressing forward. Caught hold. Continually holding fast. Those who made it to the tree did not stop and did not let go.
Elder Robert D. Hales explained what the rod stands for. In his talk "Holy Scriptures: The Power of God unto Our Salvation," from the October 2006 general conference, he said:

So essential are these truths that Heavenly Father gave both Lehi and Nephi visions vividly representing the word of God as a rod of iron. Both father and son learned that holding to this strong, unbending, utterly reliable guide is the only way to stay on that strait and narrow path that leads to our Savior.
The only way. That is a strong statement. When the road gets foggy, we hold the rod. The scriptures. The words of the prophets. Daily prayer. These are what keep us on course.
Elder Hales also spoke of the living prophet. In his talk "Hear the Prophet's Voice and Obey," from the April 1995 general conference, he said:

Our spiritual safety lies in turning to the clear voice of our living prophet. If we listen to his voice and obey his counsel, we will be able to live as Christ would have us live and endure to the end so that one day we, along with our families, will return back into the presence of our Heavenly Father and our Savior Jesus Christ.
Spiritual safety. A runner who follows the course markers does not worry about getting lost. The prophet's voice is a marker. It helps us stay where we belong.
And Paul gave a word of encouragement for when we get tired.
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
In due season. Not right away. Not every time. But in due season. The harvest comes. The finish line comes. Do not faint.
What keeps us going when the finish line is far away? Covenants.
When King Benjamin taught his people, they made a covenant to take the name of Christ. He then gave them a charge.

Therefore, I would that ye should be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in good works, that Christ, the Lord God Omnipotent, may seal you his, that you may be brought to heaven, that ye may have everlasting salvation and eternal life, through the wisdom, and power, and justice, and mercy of him who created all things, in heaven and in earth, who is God above all. Amen.

Steadfast and immovable. That is the posture of someone who intends to finish. Not the one who swings back and forth with every mood. And always abounding in good works. We do not just hold on. We do good while we hold on.

A marathon runner often keeps a pace. Not too fast, not too slow. The same is true of enduring. A regular rhythm of prayer, scripture study, and service is better than bursts of effort followed by long breaks.
Elder D. Todd Christofferson gave comfort to those who feel they are not as far along as they should be. In his talk "Born Again," from the April 2008 general conference, he said:

You may ask, Why doesn't this mighty change happen more quickly with me? . . . For most of us, the changes are more gradual and occur over time. Being born again . . . is more a process than an event. And engaging in that process is the central purpose of mortality.
The central purpose of mortality. That is why we are here. To keep walking and keep changing. Not to be perfect now, but to keep going.
What is at the finish line? The Lord has told us.
And, if you keep my commandments and endure to the end you shall have eternal life, which gift is the greatest of all the gifts of God.
Eternal life. The greatest of all the gifts of God. That is the finish line.
Paul had a moment near the end of his life when he looked back. He had been beaten, shipwrecked, jailed, and misunderstood. And this is what he wrote.

I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith: Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing.
I have finished my course. I have kept the faith. Those are the words of a runner at the finish. He did not say, I had an easy life. He said, I kept going.
And look at the last phrase. Not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing. That includes you. That includes me. The crown is not just for apostles.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when they kept going through something hard. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Paul and Silas in prison

blocks.text: Paul and Silas had been beaten and thrown into the inner prison in Philippi. Their feet were locked in stocks. It was the middle of the night. They had every reason to give up.

And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them. And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken: and immediately all the doors were opened, and every one's bands were loosed.

They prayed and sang at midnight. In the hardest hour, they did not complain. They worshipped. The other prisoners heard it. Enduring is not just about surviving. It can also be a witness to those around us.

application.text: Here are a few steps for this week.

First, find your pace. Choose one small habit that you can keep every day, even on hard days. Five minutes of scripture reading. A short prayer morning and night. Keep it small enough that you can do it when you are tired.
Second, name your mile eighteen. What is the hardest thing in your life right now? Write it down. Then write one verse from today's talk that speaks to it. Keep it where you will see it.
Third, look for someone else who is struggling to finish. Send a message. Sit with them. Run beside them for a while.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that the Lord does not ask us to run alone. I know that He has overcome the world, and that He gives strength to those who wait on Him. I have felt His help in hard times, and I have seen it in the lives of others. I know that those who endure to the end will receive eternal life. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

opening.text: A ship is built to leave the harbor. That is what ships are for. But no captain sails out thinking the sea will stay calm. Every sailor knows that storms come. The question is not whether the wind will rise. The question is what holds the ship in place when it does.

Today I want to talk about holding on. The gospel calls it enduring to the end. It is a simple idea. We keep going. We stay faithful when it is easy and when it is not. And we do it until our life is finished.
I will use a ship and an anchor to help us see it.

mainMessage.text: Enduring to the end does not mean we will have no storms. It means we will not drift. The Lord never promised smooth water. He promised that He would be with us, and that those who stay with Him will be saved.

An anchor does not stop the storm. It does not calm the waves. It holds the ship to something solid beneath it. In the same way, our faith in Jesus Christ does not take away trials. It holds us steady inside them.
Over the next few minutes we will look at six things. What enduring is. Why trials come. Where our trust belongs. How we stay on the path. What helps us keep going. And what waits for us at the end.

blocks.text: Let us start with the plain question. What does it mean to endure to the end?
The Savior said it in one sentence.
But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved.

That is the promise. Notice it is not for the one who starts well. It is for the one who endures. A ship that leaves the harbor with a fine crew and a full sail has done only half the work. The voyage is not over until it reaches the other shore.
Nephi taught the same thing, and he gave us the steps. He had just described baptism and the gift of the Holy Ghost. Then he asked a question that many of us need to hear.

And now, my beloved brethren, after ye have gotten into this strait and narrow path, I would ask if all is done? Behold, I say unto you, Nay; for ye have not come thus far save it were by the word of Christ with unshaken faith in him, relying wholly upon the merits of him who is mighty to save.
Wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life.
Is all done? Nay. Baptism is the harbor mouth, not the destination. After we step onto the path, we must press forward.

And Nephi tells us how. Steadfastness in Christ. A perfect brightness of hope. Love for God and for all people. Feasting on the word of Christ. Think of those as the supplies on the ship. Without them, the voyage is hard. With them, we can go the distance.
Now a hard truth. Storms come, even to good sailors.
Many people think that if they do what is right, life will go well. And often it does. But not always. Sometimes the faithful face the heaviest weather.
The Savior did not hide this from His disciples. On the night before He was crucified, He spoke to them.
These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.

In the world ye shall have tribulation. He said it plainly. But look at what comes before and after. In me ye might have peace. Be of good cheer. I have overcome the world. The storm is real. And He is stronger than the storm.
Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke about this in his talk "Trust in the Lord," from the October 1995 general conference. He said:

Testing . . . is needed even when you are living a worthy, righteous life and are obedient to \[God's\] commandments. Just when all seems to be going right, challenges often come in multiple doses applied simultaneously.
Multiple doses applied simultaneously. Many of us know what that feels like. A job problem, a health scare, and a family worry all in the same month. It can feel like waves from three directions.
But Elder Scott does not say this to frighten us. He says it so we will not be surprised. If we expect the storm, we are less likely to think the Lord has left us.
The Lord spoke a gentle word to the Prophet Joseph Smith when he was in Liberty Jail. Joseph was cold, hungry, and far from his family. He cried out, asking where God was. And the Lord answered him.

My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment; And then, if thou endure it well, God shall exalt thee on high; thou shalt triumph over all thy foes.

Peace be unto thy soul. A small moment. If thou endure it well. Those words did not take Joseph out of the jail that day. But they told him that the storm had an end, and that God was still at the helm.
So what is our anchor? Where do we put our trust when the waves are high?
Solomon gave a short answer that has helped people for three thousand years.
Trust in the Lord with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.

Lean not unto thine own understanding. That is hard. In a storm, we want to figure everything out. We want to see the whole map. But a ship in heavy fog cannot see the harbor. It has to trust the instruments and the chart.
Elder Scott said that trust is at the center of this life. In the same talk, "Trust in the Lord," he said:

This life is an experience in profound trust—trust in Jesus Christ. . . . To trust means to obey willingly without knowing the end from the beginning (see Prov. 3:5–7). To produce fruit, your trust in the Lord must be more powerful and enduring than your confidence in your own personal feelings and experience.
Without knowing the end from the beginning. We will not always know why a trial is happening. We may never know in this life. But we can choose to trust the One who does.
And when our own strength runs low, He gives us more.

He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength. Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall: But they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.

Even the youths shall faint. Even the strong get tired. Isaiah is honest about that. But those who wait upon the Lord get something new. Renewed strength. The word wait here does not mean sit and do nothing. It means to hold on to Him and hope in Him, and keep sailing.

There is a story in the Book of Mormon that shows how this works. Alma and his people were put under bondage by the wicked priest Amulon. They prayed. And the Lord answered, though not by removing the chains right away.

And I will also ease the burdens which are put upon your shoulders, that even you cannot feel them upon your backs, even while you are in bondage; and this will I do that ye may stand as witnesses for me hereafter, and that ye may know of a surety that I, the Lord God, do visit my people in their afflictions.
And now it came to pass that the burdens which were laid upon Alma and his brethren were made light; yea, the Lord did strengthen them that they could bear up their burdens with ease, and they did submit cheerfully and with patience to all the will of the Lord.

The burdens were made light. The chains were still there for a time. But the weight changed. The Lord strengthened them so they could bear it with ease. That is what an anchor does. It does not remove the sea. It keeps you from being swept away.
Elder Scott gave another example from the Book of Mormon. In his talk "To Be Healed," from the April 1994 general conference, he said:

The example of Alma and Amulek is enlightening. While striving to do good among the people of Ammonihah, they were taken captive. Amulek trusted his more seasoned companion, Alma, who led him to greater confidence in the Lord. Forced to observe women and children consumed by fire, Amulek said, 'Perhaps they will burn us also.' Alma answered: 'Be it according to the will of the Lord'—a vital principle. 'But . . . our work is not finished; therefore they burn us not' \[Alma 14:12–13; emphasis added\].

Be it according to the will of the Lord. Those are the words of a sailor with a deep anchor. Alma did not know how it would end. But he trusted the One who did. And notice the second half of what he said. Our work is not finished. That is a good thought for any of us in a storm. If we are still here, there is still work to do.
A ship needs more than an anchor. It needs a chart and a compass. A captain who ignores them may end up on the rocks, however good the ship.
Lehi saw a vision of a tree of life. A rod of iron ran beside a path that led to the tree. Mists of darkness came over the path. Many people let go and were lost. Others held on.

But, to be short in writing, behold, he saw other multitudes pressing forward; and they came and caught hold of the end of the rod of iron; and they did press their way forward, continually holding fast to the rod of iron, until they came forth and fell down and partook of the fruit of the tree.
Continually holding fast. Not holding on once. Not holding on when it felt good. Continually. Day after day, through the mist.
Elder Robert D. Hales taught what the rod means. In his talk "Holy Scriptures: The Power of God unto Our Salvation," from the October 2006 general conference, he said:

So essential are these truths that Heavenly Father gave both Lehi and Nephi visions vividly representing the word of God as a rod of iron. Both father and son learned that holding to this strong, unbending, utterly reliable guide is the only way to stay on that strait and narrow path that leads to our Savior.
Strong, unbending, utterly reliable. In a storm, those are the words we want. A rope made of straw will not hold. A rod of iron will. The word of God does not change with the weather.
We also have a living guide. Elder Hales spoke of that in his talk "Hear the Prophet's Voice and Obey," from the April 1995 general conference. He said:

Our spiritual safety lies in turning to the clear voice of our living prophet. If we listen to his voice and obey his counsel, we will be able to live as Christ would have us live and endure to the end so that one day we, along with our families, will return back into the presence of our Heavenly Father and our Savior Jesus Christ.
Think of the prophet's voice as a lighthouse. A lighthouse does not move the rocks. It shows where they are. When we follow its light, we stay in safe water.
And for the long nights, when we are tired and the work seems slow, Paul gave this word.
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
Let us not be weary. He does not say we will never feel weary. He says do not let weariness stop the good work. The harvest comes in due season. It may not be on our schedule, but it comes.
What is it that makes a person stay on board when leaving would be easier? A promise they have made.
When King Benjamin finished teaching his people, they made a covenant with God. They took upon them the name of Christ. And then the king gave them a charge.

Therefore, I would that ye should be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in good works, that Christ, the Lord God Omnipotent, may seal you his, that you may be brought to heaven, that ye may have everlasting salvation and eternal life, through the wisdom, and power, and justice, and mercy of him who created all things, in heaven and in earth, who is God above all. Amen.

Steadfast and immovable. That is what an anchor is. It does not swing with every wave. And always abounding in good works. A good ship does not just sit in the water. It carries something useful. We are meant to serve others while we hold on.

Some of us worry that we are not good enough at this. We slip. We drift. We wonder if we are even on the path. Elder D. Todd Christofferson spoke to that worry in his talk "Born Again," from the April 2008 general conference. He said:

You may ask, Why doesn't this mighty change happen more quickly with me? . . . For most of us, the changes are more gradual and occur over time. Being born again . . . is more a process than an event. And engaging in that process is the central purpose of mortality.

A process, not an event. A ship does not cross an ocean in one hour. It crosses by many small, steady miles. If you are still moving toward Christ, even slowly, you are doing the central work of this life.
Every voyage has a port. What is ours?
The Lord has told us in plain words.
And, if you keep my commandments and endure to the end you shall have eternal life, which gift is the greatest of all the gifts of God.
The greatest of all the gifts of God. Think about that. Out of everything God can give, this is the greatest. And it is offered to those who keep His commandments and endure to the end.
Paul wrote to Timothy near the end of his life. He was in prison again, and he knew his time was short. He looked back over the voyage.

I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith: Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing.
I have finished my course. I have kept the faith. Picture a ship coming into harbor after a long and stormy trip. The sails are worn. The hull is scarred. But the ship is home.
And Paul adds, not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing. The crown is not saved for a few great sailors. It is for everyone who keeps the faith and loves the Lord.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when they held on through a storm. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Job and the loss of everything

blocks.text: Job was a good man. In a single day he lost his property, his servants, and his children. The storm could not have been worse. Here is what he did.

Then Job arose, and rent his mantle, and shaved his head, and fell down upon the ground, and worshipped, And said, Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord. In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly.

Job grieved. He tore his robe and shaved his head. He did not pretend to feel fine. But he also fell down and worshipped. He did not blame God. His anchor held. Enduring does not mean hiding our pain. It means we bring the pain to God and not away from Him.

application.text: Here are a few ways to put this into practice.

First, check your anchor. Ask yourself what you are holding on to right now. Is it prayer? Scripture? Church? A daily habit that keeps you close to Christ? Choose one, and be steady with it this week.
Second, name your storm. Say out loud to the Lord what is hard right now. Then read one verse from today, such as John 16:33 or Isaiah 40:31, and let it be your answer for the week.
Third, be a harbor for someone else. Think of one person who is in a storm. Call them. Visit. Listen. A ship in rough water is glad to see a light on the shore.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that Jesus Christ is our anchor. I know that He has overcome the world, and that He does not leave us alone in the storm. I have felt His strength when mine was gone. I know that if we endure to the end, we will have eternal life, the greatest of all the gifts of God. I say this in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

opening.text: Have you ever seen an old tree standing alone on a hill? It has faced a hundred winters. Strong winds have bent its branches. Lightning may have scarred its trunk. Yet there it stands.
What keeps it there? Not its branches. Not its leaves. What you cannot see. The roots.
A tree on a hill does not grow deep roots in a day. It grows them slowly, a little each season, often when the weather is hard. That is a good picture of what we call enduring to the end.

mainMessage.text: Enduring is not about how loud we are when things go well. It is about how deep we are when things go wrong. Faith that has roots can bend in the wind and not break.
The Lord does not ask us to be perfect today. He asks us to keep growing toward Him, season after season, until our life is done. And He promises that those who do will be saved.
Let us look at six parts of this. What enduring means. Why the wind blows. What we trust. How we stay rooted. What feeds us. And what fruit we will have in the end.

blocks.text: What does it mean to endure to the end? The Savior said it in one line.
But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved.
Many trees sprout in spring. Not all last until the harvest. The Lord's promise is for the one who lasts. Not the one who sprouts the fastest, but the one who stays.
Nephi helps us see what this looks like in daily life. After he taught about baptism, he asked a question that is worth asking ourselves.

And now, my beloved brethren, after ye have gotten into this strait and narrow path, I would ask if all is done? Behold, I say unto you, Nay; for ye have not come thus far save it were by the word of Christ with unshaken faith in him, relying wholly upon the merits of him who is mighty to save.
Wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life.
Is all done? No. A young tree has been planted, but it is not yet grown.

Nephi names what the tree needs. Steadfastness in Christ. A perfect brightness of hope. Love of God and of everyone. And the word of Christ, which he calls a feast. These are water, sun, and soil for our souls. Without them the roots stay shallow. With them the roots go down.
Why does the wind blow? Why do trials come, even to people who are trying hard?
Some think that if they live well, they will be spared. But the Savior never taught that. On the last night before the cross, He told His friends the truth.
These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.
Tribulation is promised. But so is peace, and so is victory. The storm is real. His power is greater.
Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles gave an honest picture of this in his talk "Trust in the Lord," from the October 1995 general conference. He said:

Testing . . . is needed even when you are living a worthy, righteous life and are obedient to \[God's\] commandments. Just when all seems to be going right, challenges often come in multiple doses applied simultaneously.

Think of a tree in a winter storm. Wind, rain, and cold all arrive together. But that is also when the roots do their hardest work. A tree grown in a sheltered greenhouse looks fine, but it often cannot stand outdoors. Strength is built where the wind blows.
The Lord gave Joseph Smith a hard lesson in Liberty Jail. Joseph felt forgotten. And the Lord answered with these words.

My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment; And then, if thou endure it well, God shall exalt thee on high; thou shalt triumph over all thy foes.

If thou endure it well. That phrase is worth holding on to. The Lord does not say if you escape it. He says if you endure it well. How we go through a trial matters. The Lord promised Joseph that the hard season would pass, and that there would be victory afterward.
What do the roots of a believing person reach for? What is the soil?
Solomon described it in two short verses.
Trust in the Lord with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.

Trust. That is the soil. And it is not a trust that waits until we understand everything. Lean not unto thine own understanding. A tree does not understand how the roots find water. It simply reaches down and receives it.
Elder Scott said more about this in the same talk, "Trust in the Lord." He said:

This life is an experience in profound trust—trust in Jesus Christ. . . . To trust means to obey willingly without knowing the end from the beginning (see Prov. 3:5–7). To produce fruit, your trust in the Lord must be more powerful and enduring than your confidence in your own personal feelings and experience.

To produce fruit. Elder Scott used a tree word himself. A tree that depends only on its own feelings has roots that go only an inch deep. A tree that depends on the Lord has roots that find living water.
And when we are weak and tired, there is help.

He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength. Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall: But they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.

He giveth power to the faint. We do not have to be strong on our own. The Lord gives what we lack. And Isaiah says that even young men fall. No one is above getting tired. But those who wait upon the Lord are renewed.
The Book of Mormon gives a living example. Alma and his people were in bondage to Amulon and his men. They could not even pray aloud. Yet they poured out their hearts. And the Lord replied.

And I will also ease the burdens which are put upon your shoulders, that even you cannot feel them upon your backs, even while you are in bondage; and this will I do that ye may stand as witnesses for me hereafter, and that ye may know of a surety that I, the Lord God, do visit my people in their afflictions.
And now it came to pass that the burdens which were laid upon Alma and his brethren were made light; yea, the Lord did strengthen them that they could bear up their burdens with ease, and they did submit cheerfully and with patience to all the will of the Lord.
The Lord did not take them out right away. He strengthened them where they stood. The roots held. Later, He delivered them.
Elder Scott spoke of another pair who trusted. In his talk "To Be Healed," from the April 1994 general conference, he said:

The example of Alma and Amulek is enlightening. While striving to do good among the people of Ammonihah, they were taken captive. Amulek trusted his more seasoned companion, Alma, who led him to greater confidence in the Lord. Forced to observe women and children consumed by fire, Amulek said, 'Perhaps they will burn us also.' Alma answered: 'Be it according to the will of the Lord'—a vital principle. 'But . . . our work is not finished; therefore they burn us not' \[Alma 14:12–13; emphasis added\].

Notice how Amulek leaned on someone with deeper roots. That is a good lesson. Sometimes our faith is thin, and we need a friend, a parent, or a leader whose roots are deeper to lean on for a while. And one day we may be that friend for someone else.
How does a tree stay upright in a gale? It stays anchored to the ground it grows in. How do we stay anchored? By holding to what does not move.
In Lehi's dream, there was a rod of iron beside the path to the tree of life. Dark mists rolled in. Some people lost their way. But Nephi writes of others who did something different.

But, to be short in writing, behold, he saw other multitudes pressing forward; and they came and caught hold of the end of the rod of iron; and they did press their way forward, continually holding fast to the rod of iron, until they came forth and fell down and partook of the fruit of the tree.
They caught hold. They pressed forward. They kept holding fast. And in the end they ate the fruit. A tree that endures bears fruit. So does a person.
Elder Robert D. Hales explained what the rod represents. In his talk "Holy Scriptures: The Power of God unto Our Salvation," from the October 2006 general conference, he said:

So essential are these truths that Heavenly Father gave both Lehi and Nephi visions vividly representing the word of God as a rod of iron. Both father and son learned that holding to this strong, unbending, utterly reliable guide is the only way to stay on that strait and narrow path that leads to our Savior.
The only way. That means no shortcuts. The way to stay on the path is to hold the word of God. Read it. Pray over it. Let it shape what we choose each day. That is how roots go down.
Elder Hales also pointed us to a living voice. In his talk "Hear the Prophet's Voice and Obey," from the April 1995 general conference, he said:

Our spiritual safety lies in turning to the clear voice of our living prophet. If we listen to his voice and obey his counsel, we will be able to live as Christ would have us live and endure to the end so that one day we, along with our families, will return back into the presence of our Heavenly Father and our Savior Jesus Christ.

Spiritual safety. A young tree is often tied to a stake so that wind cannot snap it before the roots are deep. The counsel of the prophet can be like that stake. It keeps us upright while we are still growing.
And Paul adds a quiet word of encouragement for the long wait.
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
A farmer knows this verse well. You plant, you water, you wait. You do not dig up the seed every week to see if it is growing. In due season the harvest comes, if we do not faint.
What feeds the roots day after day? Our covenants, kept with care.
When King Benjamin's people covenanted to take upon them the name of Christ, he closed his sermon with this charge.

Therefore, I would that ye should be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in good works, that Christ, the Lord God Omnipotent, may seal you his, that you may be brought to heaven, that ye may have everlasting salvation and eternal life, through the wisdom, and power, and justice, and mercy of him who created all things, in heaven and in earth, who is God above all. Amen.

Steadfast and immovable. Like a tree with deep roots. And always abounding in good works. A healthy tree does not only stand. It gives shade, fruit, and shelter to others. A faithful life does the same.
Some of us look at our lives and feel we are growing too slowly. Elder D. Todd Christofferson spoke to that feeling in his talk "Born Again," from the April 2008 general conference. He said:

You may ask, Why doesn't this mighty change happen more quickly with me? . . . For most of us, the changes are more gradual and occur over time. Being born again . . . is more a process than an event. And engaging in that process is the central purpose of mortality.
No one watches a tree and sees it grow. But a year later, it is taller. Change in us is like that. It is slow, quiet, and real. If you are still reaching for Christ, you are growing.
What fruit waits at the end? The Lord has named it.
And, if you keep my commandments and endure to the end you shall have eternal life, which gift is the greatest of all the gifts of God.
Eternal life is the fruit. It is the greatest gift that God has to give. And it comes to those who keep His commandments and endure.
Paul wrote his last letter from a prison cell. He knew his death was near. And he did not write in fear. He wrote in peace.

I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith: Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing.
I have kept the faith. That is what a long life of faith sounds like. Not boastful. Just settled. Paul had been through storms, and he was still standing.
And again, not to me only. The crown is for all who love His appearing. If you love the Lord and are trying to follow Him, that includes you.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when their faith stayed firm under pressure. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Daniel in the lions' den

blocks.text: Daniel prayed to God three times a day, even after the king made a law against it. He was thrown into a den of lions. He had done nothing wrong. In the morning the king came to the den and called to him.

My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me: forasmuch as before him innocency was found in me; and also before thee, O king, have I done no hurt. Then was the king exceeding glad for him, and commanded that they should take Daniel up out of the den. So Daniel was taken up out of the den, and no manner of hurt was found upon him, because he believed in his God.

Daniel's roots had grown deep long before the night in the den. He had prayed every day for years. When the storm came, he did not have to build his faith from scratch. He used what was already there. Our daily habits now become our strength later.

application.text: Here are some ways to grow deeper this week.
First, water the roots. Pick one small thing you will do each day without fail. Pray at the same time each morning. Read a few verses before bed. Small habits dig deep over time.
Second, find your stake. Who is someone with stronger roots that you can lean on? A leader, a parent, a friend. Reach out to them this week and tell them what you are facing.
Third, be shade for someone. Look for a person who is worn out by the wind. Offer a visit, a meal, or a kind word. Strong trees shelter others.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that the Savior is the source of living water. I know that when we keep our roots in Him, we will not be moved. I have seen His hand in the hard seasons of my life. I know that those who endure to the end will have eternal life. I say this in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

opening.text: Imagine driving through a long mountain tunnel. At the start, the entrance is bright behind you. Then the road bends, and the daylight is gone. For a while, all you see are the taillights ahead and the dim lamps on the wall.

A good driver does not panic. They know the tunnel has an end. They keep their hands on the wheel, keep their eyes on the road, and keep going. Soon a small bright spot appears ahead. It grows. And then they are out in the sun.
Life has tunnels. Today I want to talk about how to get through them.

mainMessage.text: The gospel calls this enduring to the end. It means we stay faithful through the dark stretches. It means we do not turn around in the middle of the tunnel. The Lord promises that the light at the other end is real, and that He is with us in the dark.

We will look at six things. What it means to endure. Why the tunnel is part of the road. Who we trust when we cannot see. What keeps us moving. What our promises do. And the light that waits at the end.

blocks.text: First, what is enduring? Jesus gave a short answer.
But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved.
Saved is the promise. Endure is the condition. A driver who stops halfway through the tunnel does not reach the other side. We have to keep moving.
Nephi saw that some people think the work is done after baptism. He answered them directly.

And now, my beloved brethren, after ye have gotten into this strait and narrow path, I would ask if all is done? Behold, I say unto you, Nay; for ye have not come thus far save it were by the word of Christ with unshaken faith in him, relying wholly upon the merits of him who is mighty to save.
Wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life.

Nephi says, a perfect brightness of hope. That is the light in the tunnel. Even when we cannot see the end, we carry a brightness in us. It comes from Christ. It does not depend on the road around us.
Press forward. Keep feasting on His word. Keep loving God and others. That is how we travel.
Why is there a tunnel at all? Why does the Lord let hard things happen to people who are trying to follow Him?
He never hid this from us. On the night of the Last Supper, Jesus told His disciples what to expect.
These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.
He told them ahead of time. Tribulation is part of living in this world. But look at what He offers. Peace in Him. Good cheer. And the fact that He has already overcome.
Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles gave a clear explanation in his talk "Trust in the Lord," from the October 1995 general conference. He said:

Testing . . . is needed even when you are living a worthy, righteous life and are obedient to \[God's\] commandments. Just when all seems to be going right, challenges often come in multiple doses applied simultaneously.
This helps us. When hard things pile up, we do not need to think we did something wrong. Sometimes a tunnel is just the shape of the mountain. Even the faithful go through it.
The Prophet Joseph Smith went through a long, dark tunnel in Liberty Jail. For months he sat in a cold cell. And the Lord spoke to him there.

My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment; And then, if thou endure it well, God shall exalt thee on high; thou shalt triumph over all thy foes.

A small moment. In the middle of a tunnel, it feels endless. But the Lord sees the whole road, and He calls it a small moment. And He adds, if thou endure it well. We can choose to go through it with faith, patience, and trust.
When we cannot see ahead, whom do we trust? The one who can.
Trust in the Lord with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.
He shall direct thy paths. A driver in a tunnel trusts the road signs and the engineers who built it. We trust the One who built the path and walked it first.
Elder Scott taught that trust is the heart of this life. In the same talk, "Trust in the Lord," he said:

This life is an experience in profound trust—trust in Jesus Christ. . . . To trust means to obey willingly without knowing the end from the beginning (see Prov. 3:5–7). To produce fruit, your trust in the Lord must be more powerful and enduring than your confidence in your own personal feelings and experience.
Our own feelings can be unreliable in the dark. We may feel alone even when we are not. Elder Scott invites us to trust the Lord more than we trust our feelings of the moment.
And when our strength runs out, He gives us more.

He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength. Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall: But they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.

Three stages are named here. Run. Walk. Not faint. Some days we can run. Some days we can only walk. And on the hardest days, the promise is that we will not faint. We will not fall. That is enough to get through a tunnel.
The Lord gave this kind of help to Alma and his people when they were held in bondage. They could not escape. But they could pray in their hearts. And the Lord answered.

And I will also ease the burdens which are put upon your shoulders, that even you cannot feel them upon your backs, even while you are in bondage; and this will I do that ye may stand as witnesses for me hereafter, and that ye may know of a surety that I, the Lord God, do visit my people in their afflictions.
And now it came to pass that the burdens which were laid upon Alma and his brethren were made light; yea, the Lord did strengthen them that they could bear up their burdens with ease, and they did submit cheerfully and with patience to all the will of the Lord.
The Lord did not shorten the tunnel. He lightened the load. They carried the same burdens, but they carried them with ease. If you are in a dark stretch now, you can ask for that kind of help.
Elder Scott shared one more story from the Book of Mormon. In his talk "To Be Healed," from the April 1994 general conference, he said:

The example of Alma and Amulek is enlightening. While striving to do good among the people of Ammonihah, they were taken captive. Amulek trusted his more seasoned companion, Alma, who led him to greater confidence in the Lord. Forced to observe women and children consumed by fire, Amulek said, 'Perhaps they will burn us also.' Alma answered: 'Be it according to the will of the Lord'—a vital principle. 'But . . . our work is not finished; therefore they burn us not' \[Alma 14:12–13; emphasis added\].
Our work is not finished. When we are in the tunnel, those words can steady us. Our task is not to understand it all. Our task is to keep doing what the Lord asked of us, until He brings us out.
In a tunnel, what keeps a driver from drifting into the wall? The lane lines, and the lights along the side. They show where to go when the view is poor.
The Lord has given us the same kind of guide. In Lehi's dream, a rod of iron ran along the path. Mists of darkness covered the way. Some walked into the mist and were lost. But others held on.

But, to be short in writing, behold, he saw other multitudes pressing forward; and they came and caught hold of the end of the rod of iron; and they did press their way forward, continually holding fast to the rod of iron, until they came forth and fell down and partook of the fruit of the tree.

They pressed their way forward. That phrase tells us it took effort. They did not float to the tree. They held the rod and pushed on, step by step, in the dark, until they came out and tasted the fruit.
Elder Robert D. Hales told us what the rod stands for. In his talk "Holy Scriptures: The Power of God unto Our Salvation," from the October 2006 general conference, he said:

So essential are these truths that Heavenly Father gave both Lehi and Nephi visions vividly representing the word of God as a rod of iron. Both father and son learned that holding to this strong, unbending, utterly reliable guide is the only way to stay on that strait and narrow path that leads to our Savior.

The word of God is the lane line in the dark. It does not depend on how we feel on a given day. It is unbending. It is reliable. When the mist is thick, we do not need to see everything. We need to hold on.
Elder Hales also taught us to listen for a living voice. In his talk "Hear the Prophet's Voice and Obey," from the April 1995 general conference, he said:

Our spiritual safety lies in turning to the clear voice of our living prophet. If we listen to his voice and obey his counsel, we will be able to live as Christ would have us live and endure to the end so that one day we, along with our families, will return back into the presence of our Heavenly Father and our Savior Jesus Christ.
The prophet's counsel is like the voice of a traffic officer at the tunnel entrance. He can see things we cannot. When he says go slowly, or keep to the right, it is for our safety.
And when the tunnel feels long, we have Paul's encouragement.
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
You may feel weary. That is normal. Paul does not scold us for it. He just reminds us not to quit. In due season, the reward comes.
What gives a person the will to keep driving through the dark? Often it is a promise made and a promise remembered.
When King Benjamin's people entered a covenant with God, he gave them a final instruction.

Therefore, I would that ye should be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in good works, that Christ, the Lord God Omnipotent, may seal you his, that you may be brought to heaven, that ye may have everlasting salvation and eternal life, through the wisdom, and power, and justice, and mercy of him who created all things, in heaven and in earth, who is God above all. Amen.

Steadfast. Immovable. Always doing good. It is a steady kind of faith. Not flashy. Not always felt. But steady. The one who keeps their covenants in the dark is the one who will come out into the light.

Some of us worry that we are going too slowly. We wish the change in us would come faster. Elder D. Todd Christofferson addressed this directly in his talk "Born Again," from the April 2008 general conference. He said:

You may ask, Why doesn't this mighty change happen more quickly with me? . . . For most of us, the changes are more gradual and occur over time. Being born again . . . is more a process than an event. And engaging in that process is the central purpose of mortality.
Gradual. Over time. A long tunnel is not crossed at once. It is crossed one mile marker after another. You do not have to be done. You only have to be moving.
What is the light at the end of the tunnel? The Lord told us.
And, if you keep my commandments and endure to the end you shall have eternal life, which gift is the greatest of all the gifts of God.
Eternal life. Not just life after death, but life with God and our families, in a state of joy. The Lord calls it the greatest of all His gifts. No tunnel is too long for that.
Paul knew what it was to travel through dark places. Shipwreck. Prison. Stones. And at the end he wrote this.

I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith: Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing.

I have finished my course. He came out of the tunnel. And what he saw was light. A crown of righteousness. He says it is laid up. It is waiting. And it is waiting for all who love the Lord, not for Paul alone.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when they came through a dark stretch with faith. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Alma and Amulek freed from prison

blocks.text: Alma and Amulek had been bound, beaten, and kept in prison for many days. They had watched innocent people die. They were weak and hungry. And then Alma prayed.

And Alma cried, saying: How long shall we suffer these great afflictions, O Lord? O Lord, give us strength according to our faith which is in Christ, even unto deliverance. And they broke the cords with which they were bound; and when the people saw this, they began to flee, for the fear of destruction had come upon them.

Alma did not hide his weariness. How long, O Lord? That is an honest prayer. But he also asked for strength according to his faith in Christ. He asked for help to keep going. The cords broke. Later in the chapter, the prison walls fell, and the two walked out unhurt, because the Lord had given them power according to their faith. The light was at the end of the tunnel. They had to walk through to reach it.

application.text: Here are some simple steps for this week.
First, check your lights. What are the lights along your road right now? Scripture, prayer, a church calling, a good friend? Make sure each one is turned on. Spend a little time with each.
Second, say the honest prayer. If you are in a tunnel, tell the Lord, "How long?" Then ask, "Give me strength." He is not offended by honest prayers.
Third, shine for someone else. Is there someone near you who is in the dark? Send a message. Pray for them by name. A small light helps more than you think.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that the Lord is the light at the end of every dark road. I know that He walks with us through the tunnel, even when we cannot see Him. I have felt His peace when everything around me was uncertain. I know that those who endure to the end will have eternal life. I say this in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

opening.text: If you have flown much, you know the moment. The plane is cruising smoothly. Then, without warning, it drops and shakes. Cups rattle. Someone gasps. The seatbelt sign comes on.

Here is what experienced travelers know. Turbulence feels dangerous, but a well-built plane is made for it. The pilot has flown through it before. The best thing a passenger can do is stay seated, stay buckled, and trust the one in the cockpit.
Today's talk is about staying buckled in. The Lord calls it enduring to the end.

mainMessage.text: None of us flies through life on smooth air the whole way. Some hit the bumps early. Some hit them late. But everyone gets some. What matters is whether we stay with the Savior when the plane shakes.

Enduring to the end is staying with Christ from the moment we first commit to Him until our life is finished. He has promised that those who do will be saved. He has not promised a quiet flight. He has promised that He is the pilot, and that He knows the way home.
We will look at six parts of this idea. What endurance is. Why the air gets rough. Who we trust in the cockpit. How we stay safe in our seats. What we hold in our hands. And where the flight lands.

blocks.text: Let us begin with the Savior's own words.
But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved.
That is the whole flight plan in one sentence. We are not saved by takeoff. We are saved by arrival. A plane that takes off beautifully but never lands has not completed the trip.
Nephi gave us a fuller picture. After he taught about the first steps of the gospel, he asked whether we were done. His answer was no.

And now, my beloved brethren, after ye have gotten into this strait and narrow path, I would ask if all is done? Behold, I say unto you, Nay; for ye have not come thus far save it were by the word of Christ with unshaken faith in him, relying wholly upon the merits of him who is mighty to save.
Wherefore, ye must press forward with a steadfastness in Christ, having a perfect brightness of hope, and a love of God and of all men. Wherefore, if ye shall press forward, feasting upon the word of Christ, and endure to the end, behold, thus saith the Father: Ye shall have eternal life.
Baptism puts us on the plane. Pressing forward keeps us flying. Nephi says to rely wholly upon the merits of him who is mighty to save. That means we rest our weight on Christ, not on our own record.
And notice what he asks us to bring on board. Steadfastness. Hope. Love. And a steady diet of the word of Christ. These are what make for a calm cabin even when the air is rough.
Why does the air get rough? Why does the Lord allow hard things for people who are trying to do right?
He told His disciples plainly that it would happen.
These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.
The Savior gives a warning, a comfort, and a promise in one breath. Warning: tribulation will come. Comfort: you can have peace in Him. Promise: He has already overcome the world.
Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles explained this in his talk "Trust in the Lord," from the October 1995 general conference. He said:

Testing . . . is needed even when you are living a worthy, righteous life and are obedient to \[God's\] commandments. Just when all seems to be going right, challenges often come in multiple doses applied simultaneously.
Multiple doses at once. That is turbulence. It does not come one bump at a time. Sometimes it feels like the whole plane is shaking.
But Elder Scott does not tell us this to scare us. He tells us so that when the shaking starts, we do not conclude that God has left the cockpit. He has not.
Joseph Smith was held in Liberty Jail through a bitter winter. He felt forgotten and cried out to God. The Lord's answer is one of the most comforting in all of scripture.

My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment; And then, if thou endure it well, God shall exalt thee on high; thou shalt triumph over all thy foes.
Peace be unto thy soul. Before the Lord explained anything, He gave peace. Then He said it would be a small moment. And then He gave the instruction. Endure it well. Stay buckled in.
Who do we trust when the plane drops? The pilot.
A passenger cannot see the instruments. We cannot read the radar. We do not know the weather ahead. We have to trust the one who can.
Trust in the Lord with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.
Lean not unto thine own understanding. Passengers who try to fly the plane from their seat do not help. We are called to trust. And He shall direct thy paths. The pilot knows the route.
Elder Scott taught that this trust is the core of life. In the same talk, "Trust in the Lord," he said:

This life is an experience in profound trust—trust in Jesus Christ. . . . To trust means to obey willingly without knowing the end from the beginning (see Prov. 3:5–7). To produce fruit, your trust in the Lord must be more powerful and enduring than your confidence in your own personal feelings and experience.

Without knowing the end from the beginning. A passenger does not know when the shaking will stop. But a passenger can choose to believe the pilot. Our trust does not depend on seeing the whole flight plan.
And when we feel too tired to hold on, there is a promise.

He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength. Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall: But they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.

Mount up with wings as eagles. An eagle uses storm winds to climb higher. It does not fight the wind. It lets the wind lift it. Isaiah says that those who wait upon the Lord can rise in the very conditions that frighten others.
The Book of Mormon tells of Alma and his people under bondage, and how the Lord helped them bear it.

And I will also ease the burdens which are put upon your shoulders, that even you cannot feel them upon your backs, even while you are in bondage; and this will I do that ye may stand as witnesses for me hereafter, and that ye may know of a surety that I, the Lord God, do visit my people in their afflictions.
And now it came to pass that the burdens which were laid upon Alma and his brethren were made light; yea, the Lord did strengthen them that they could bear up their burdens with ease, and they did submit cheerfully and with patience to all the will of the Lord.
With ease and with patience. The bumps did not stop at once. But the Lord changed how the people felt them. He can do the same for us.
Elder Scott gave another Book of Mormon example. In his talk "To Be Healed," from the April 1994 general conference, he said:

The example of Alma and Amulek is enlightening. While striving to do good among the people of Ammonihah, they were taken captive. Amulek trusted his more seasoned companion, Alma, who led him to greater confidence in the Lord. Forced to observe women and children consumed by fire, Amulek said, 'Perhaps they will burn us also.' Alma answered: 'Be it according to the will of the Lord'—a vital principle. 'But . . . our work is not finished; therefore they burn us not' \[Alma 14:12–13; emphasis added\].

Be it according to the will of the Lord. That is a calm voice in a shaking cabin. Alma did not demand an easy flight. He accepted whatever the Lord allowed, and he trusted that the work was not finished.
What keeps a passenger safe in turbulence? A seatbelt, and staying in the seat. What keeps us safe on the path? Holding to what is fixed.
Lehi's dream shows this. A rod of iron ran beside the path to the tree of life. Mist covered the way. Some let go and wandered. Some did not.

But, to be short in writing, behold, he saw other multitudes pressing forward; and they came and caught hold of the end of the rod of iron; and they did press their way forward, continually holding fast to the rod of iron, until they came forth and fell down and partook of the fruit of the tree.
The word to notice is continually. Not once, not for a week. They kept hold through the whole walk. And the reward was the fruit of the tree.
Elder Robert D. Hales explained the rod in his talk "Holy Scriptures: The Power of God unto Our Salvation," from the October 2006 general conference. He said:

So essential are these truths that Heavenly Father gave both Lehi and Nephi visions vividly representing the word of God as a rod of iron. Both father and son learned that holding to this strong, unbending, utterly reliable guide is the only way to stay on that strait and narrow path that leads to our Savior.
Unbending and reliable. When the plane shakes, we want something solid to grab. The word of God is that. We read it, we pray over it, and we let it steer our choices.
Elder Hales also taught about the living prophet. In his talk "Hear the Prophet's Voice and Obey," from the April 1995 general conference, he said:

Our spiritual safety lies in turning to the clear voice of our living prophet. If we listen to his voice and obey his counsel, we will be able to live as Christ would have us live and endure to the end so that one day we, along with our families, will return back into the presence of our Heavenly Father and our Savior Jesus Christ.
Spiritual safety. When the captain speaks over the speaker, passengers listen. The prophet's voice is like that. It tells us what we need to do now, in the weather we are in.
And Paul reminds us to stay at it, even when we are tired.
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
Well doing means the small, good things. Prayer. Kindness. Service. They may seem small in a storm. But they add up. In due season, we shall reap.
What do we hold in our hands while the cabin shakes? Our covenants.
When King Benjamin's people took the name of Christ, he gave them a charge.

Therefore, I would that ye should be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in good works, that Christ, the Lord God Omnipotent, may seal you his, that you may be brought to heaven, that ye may have everlasting salvation and eternal life, through the wisdom, and power, and justice, and mercy of him who created all things, in heaven and in earth, who is God above all. Amen.

Steadfast and immovable. It is a calm word in a shaking world. And the king adds always abounding in good works. A calm passenger can also help the one beside them. We stay steady, and we help others stay steady too.
Some of us feel we are not doing this well enough. Elder D. Todd Christofferson spoke to that in his talk "Born Again," from the April 2008 general conference. He said:

You may ask, Why doesn't this mighty change happen more quickly with me? . . . For most of us, the changes are more gradual and occur over time. Being born again . . . is more a process than an event. And engaging in that process is the central purpose of mortality.
A process. A long flight is many hours. You do not arrive at the first one. If you are still in your seat, still headed home, you are doing what the Lord asks.
Where does the flight land? The Lord has told us.
And, if you keep my commandments and endure to the end you shall have eternal life, which gift is the greatest of all the gifts of God.
Eternal life is the landing. It is the greatest gift that God can give. It is worth every bump on the way.
Paul knew this. At the end of a hard life, he wrote to Timothy.

I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith: Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing.

I have finished my course. Paul had been through many storms. But he stayed with the Lord, and at the end he could say he had finished. He speaks of a crown that is laid up. And it is not only for him. It is for all who love the Lord's appearing. That is an invitation to each of us.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time when they stayed with the Lord through a shaking season. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Jesus in Gethsemane

blocks.text: The greatest example of enduring is the Savior Himself. On the night before His death, He went into a garden to pray, knowing what was ahead.

And he was withdrawn from them about a stone's cast, and kneeled down, and prayed, Saying, Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done. And there appeared an angel unto him from heaven, strengthening him. And being in an agony he prayed more earnestly: and his sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground.

He did not pretend it was easy. He asked if there was another way. But He ended with, not my will, but thine, be done. And an angel strengthened Him. When we pray in our own gardens, the same help is offered. We may not be spared the hard thing. But we will not be left alone in it. And He, who endured all things, is able to help us endure.

application.text: Here are a few steps to take this week.

First, stay buckled in. Choose one thing that keeps you close to the Lord when things get rough. Maybe it is a daily prayer, a Sunday habit, or a verse on your phone. Hold to it, even when you do not feel like it.
Second, pray the Gethsemane prayer. When something hard is in front of you, tell the Lord how you feel. Then say, not my will, but thine, be done. Ask for an angel's help, in whatever form it comes.
Third, speak a calm word. Someone near you is shaking right now. A short message, a visit, or a quiet prayer for them may be what keeps them in their seat.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that Jesus Christ is the one who endured all things for us. I know that He is at the controls, and that He will bring us home if we stay with Him. I have felt His peace in rough times. I know that those who endure to the end will have eternal life. I say this in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.
